Mining · Zambia · The Copperbelt and North-Western Province

Know what is changing on and around your mining licence area in Zambia

Mining-right holders in Zambia need written consent before working near homes, railways and village land, and landholders under an exploration licence may not build without the licence holder’s consent. AfriScan gives you a dated register of structures, pits, spoil and cleared ground inside and around your licence area, so land, community and security teams share one set of facts. A person reviews every result.

Send us your licence boundary See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Consent distances fixed in law, land that keeps changing

MRC Act 2024, s.35

“We need consent before we work near those houses.”

A rights holder needs the owner’s or occupier’s written consent before working within 180 m of an occupied house or building, and the consent of the chief and the local authority on village or customary land. A register of what stands where, and since when, is where those conversations start.

MRC Act 2024, s.37(2)

“New houses appear on our exploration licence.”

An owner or occupier of land under an exploration licence “shall not erect a building or structure on the land without the consent of the holder of the exploration licence”. Knowing when each structure first appears keeps later compensation talks grounded.

Artisanal digging

“Pits keep opening at the edge of the licence area.”

Artisanal digging shows up as pits, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations, often along the licence boundary or on old workings. Mapping the ground between dates shows where it is spreading and where it has stopped.

Expansions and resettlement

“The expansion footprint needs a baseline.”

A new pit, dump or tailings facility changes who is affected. A dated record of the structures inside the new footprint is needed before the census and before the cut-off date is announced.

Who this is for

  • Mine land and surface-rights managers
  • Social-performance and community-relations teams
  • Security and asset-protection teams, as users of land-change data
  • Tailings engineers and emergency-preparedness managers
  • Resettlement and RAP teams
  • Exploration and project-development teams
  • Mine surveyors and GIS teams

The Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024

Where a rights holder needs consent before working

The Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024 (No. 14 of 2024) repeals the Mines and Minerals Development Act 2015 (s.97(1)); licences granted earlier stay valid until they expire (s.97(2)), and the Commission’s first licensing committee met on 17 June 2026. Under s.35, a rights holder may not work without written consent:

Near Distance Whose consent
An inhabited, occupied or temporarily uninhabited house or building 180 m The owner or occupier
Cleared or cropped land 45 m The owner or occupier
A cattle dip tank, dam or private water 90 m The owner or occupier
A building or dam owned by the Republic 90 m The appropriate authority
Railway land, or within 100 m of any railway track 100 m from the track The railway administration
City, municipal or district boundaries 60 m The local authority
Village or customary land The chief and the local authority for the district

The section also covers burial grounds, monuments, Government aerodromes, forests, streets and roads, national parks, game management areas and bird sanctuaries, and land that needs planning permission.

Section 37(2) adds that landholders under an exploration licence may not build without the licence holder’s consent, with the Commission able to grant consent that is unreasonably withheld, and s.40 requires “fair and reasonable compensation” for disturbance and for damage to crops, trees and buildings, with claims within three years. No exploration, mining, processing or gold panning may take place without a right and prior ZEMA approval of the environmental impact assessment (s.10), and artisanal mining is reserved to citizens and co-operatives wholly composed of citizens (s.20). Each of those rules is easier to apply with a dated register of what is on the land. For the full picture of wayleaves, reserves and consents, see our wayleave guide.

Licence areas and boundaries

What stands inside your licence area, and in a ring around it

We list the structures inside your licence area and in a ring around it, and the structures within the consent distances around your planned pits, dumps and haul roads. Each record carries its location, its distance to the boundary or feature, its band and the imagery date. New structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the boundary are mapped between dates and confirmed by a reviewer; on drone imagery, a reviewer checks fence lines and gates, which are too thin to find automatically on satellite imagery.

We work from the boundary you give us, such as the licence area from the mining cadastre or your own survey, and do not verify title, tenure or surface rights. A boundary that needs surveying or beaconing is a land surveyor’s work.

What you receive

  • A licence-area register: structures inside the boundary and in a ring around it
  • Structures within the s.35 distances you choose
  • New structures, cleared ground and tracks at the boundary between dates
  • A structure layer across the whole licence area
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Artisanal digging as ground disturbance

Pits, spoil and disturbed ground on and around your licence area

New pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground inside and around your licence area are mapped from dated imagery, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. Tracks leading to them are mapped the same way, so your teams can see how sites are reached and where activity is spreading, moving or stopping. In the rainy season, radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check.

What we map is the ground. We do not identify, count or follow people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above. Flagged sites are indications for your teams to check, not proof of anything, and whether and how to act on them is your decision, taken with the authorities and the communities around the licence area. Where formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining is on the table under the Geological and Minerals Development Act 2025, the same dated maps show where digging has taken place and how the ground has changed.

Excavation mapping

  • Pits, spoil heaps and water-filled excavations
  • New and expanding sites between dated surveys
  • Tracks to and between sites
  • Radar screening for larger changes in the rainy season
  • Every flagged site confirmed by a reviewer

Artisanal mining and excavation mapping

Tailings, blast and hazard zones

A current list of the structures inside the zones your engineers define

You supply the zones: the inundation area from a dam-break study, a blast exclusion radius, a flood line or a safety setback. We list each structure the review confirms inside them, with its location, its distance to the source and its band, and show how settlement inside each zone changes between surveys. Where compounds are dense or roofs are hard to read, reviewers mark structures by hand on high-resolution imagery.

On request, we add estimated households derived from the structure counts, with the assumptions stated, for preparedness planning and engagement. Zones are re-surveyed on the schedule you agree with us, with a notice after each survey saying what changed.

What this register is, and isn’t

A list of structures in the zones you define, with the imagery date on every record. It is not a dam-break model, a dam-safety assessment or a statement of conformance with any tailings standard, and it counts structures, not people at risk.

Expansions and resettlement

Record the footprint before the census

When a pit, dump, plant or tailings facility expands, we produce a dated record of the structures inside the new footprint, with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction, and on request estimated households. We found no stand-alone resettlement statute in Zambia; compensation runs through the Lands Acquisition Act and s.40 of the Minerals Regulation Commission Act, and lender-financed projects add IFC Performance Standard 5. Our record supports the census and asset inventory and the cut-off-date records; it does not replace them, and categories do not establish use, ownership or value.

After the cut-off date, dated re-surveys show what has appeared in the footprint since, and a location check pulls every dated image of a single plot when a claim needs it.

Your drone imagery, our analysis

Already flying drones? We analyse your own imagery

ZCAA’s published list of ROC holders includes a mining company that flies its own drones. If your survey team already produces orthophotos, send them: we run the structure register, the excavation mapping, the boundary analysis and the change detection on them, have a person review every result, and return the register and GIS layers in the formats your GIS team uses. Between flights, or over the parts of the licence area you do not fly, dated satellite scenes show what changed where they exist.

Where you want new drone surveys, they are subject to the ZCAA approvals and Zambia Air Force clearance each operation requires. On a mine site that also means your pass: the consolidated Protected Places and Areas Act prints an order that makes mine workings protected places (whether it is still in force is for Zambian counsel), and any drone work on site is flown with your pass and permissions. Afridrone is working towards the ZCAA approvals Zambia requires.

Drone law in Zambia

The ROC and Air Services Permit, the special authorisation for each operation, the 50 m rules and the protected-places orders that cover mine workings.

For procurement teams

Mining local content and supplier status

The Geological and Minerals Development (Local Content) Regulations, SI 68 of 2025, in force since 1 January 2026, require mining companies to reserve a growing share of their procurement for local companies, meaning citizen-owned or citizen-empowered companies, and reserve some non-core goods and services critical to mining for them. Which category remote-sensing and mapping work falls into is a question for counsel. Our notes for procurement teams set out the rules; each proposal states the contracting structure for your tender.

How it works

From licence boundary to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the licence-area boundary, planned workings and any zones your engineers use, tell us what you already fly and what the register is for. We agree the bands, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Map from satellite or your imagery

    Dated satellite scenes, open building datasets or your own orthophotos give the first register of structures, pits and tracks.

  3. Review

    A person checks every result before anything is delivered; what imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

  4. Deliver and repeat

    The report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name, and re-surveys follow the schedule you set.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, pits, spoil, tracks and cleared ground visible from the air
  • Report structures within the consent distances and zones you choose
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Analyse the drone imagery you already fly

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people, or say who is digging
  • See underground workings, or verify title and tenure
  • Model dam breaks, blasts or floods, or assess dam safety
  • Decide whether consent was given or a site is lawful

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging on our licence area?

No. We map the ground, such as pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. We never identify or count people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above. What the sites mean, and what to do about them, is for your teams and the authorities.

What does the 180 m rule mean for our register?

Section 35 of the Minerals Regulation Commission Act 2024 says a rights holder may not work within 180 m of an inhabited, occupied or temporarily uninhabited house or building without the owner’s or occupier’s written consent. We can report the structures within 180 m of your planned workings, pits or haul roads as a band in the register, with the imagery date. Which buildings count, and whose consent is needed, is for your land and legal teams.

Someone has built on our exploration licence. Can you show when?

We can show when a structure first appears in the dated imagery available for the site, which is often what a land team needs. Section 37(2) of the Act says an owner or occupier of land under an exploration licence may not erect a building or structure without the licence holder’s consent, and the Commission may grant consent that is unreasonably withheld. Whether consent was given is outside what imagery shows.

Our mine workings may be a protected place. Can you still map our site?

Yes, for you or with your written authority. The consolidated Protected Places and Areas Act prints an order that makes all places, excavations or works where mining is carried on protected places, with passes from the licence holder’s representative; whether that order is still in force in the 2019 Revised Edition is for Zambian counsel. Satellite work involves no one on site; any drone flight is flown with your pass and permissions, and security features are masked in every deliverable.

Do you model tailings dam breaks or blast zones?

No. Your engineers supply the zones, from the dam-break study, the blast design or your emergency plan. We list the structures inside them, each with its location and distance to the source, and show how settlement inside them changes between surveys.

We already fly our own drones. Can you use our imagery?

Yes. ZCAA’s published list of ROC holders includes a mining company that flies its own drones, and many survey teams already produce orthophotos on a cycle. Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs and we run the same structure, excavation and boundary analysis on them, with a reviewer confirming every result. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality, which we check on a sample first.

Can your baseline replace our resettlement census?

No. A dated record of the structures in an expansion footprint supports your census and asset inventory and, where lenders apply it, the IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records. Categories describe what the imagery shows; compensation needs ground verification.

Send us your licence boundary

The licence-area boundary, planned pits, dumps and haul roads, and any tailings or blast zones your engineers use (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON). Tell us what you already fly and what the register is for. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
